title: One Rank-1 LoRA = Self-Awareness? Testing the Minimal-Mechanism Claim
quick_reasoning: Directly probes a safety-relevant self-awareness mechanism, reasonably scoped.

original_idea.body:
# One Rank-1 LoRA = Self-Awareness? Testing the Minimal-Mechanism Claim

**Problem:** "Minimal and Mechanistic Conditions for Behavioral Self-Awareness in LLMs" (arXiv:2511.04875) claims self-awareness can be induced with a single rank-1 LoRA adapter and captured by one steering vector. This striking minimality claim invites a cheap independent replication on a different small open model.

**Direction:** On a small open model, induce a simple learned behavior, then attempt to elicit self-aware verbalization using progressively smaller adapters (rank-8 → rank-1). Extract a steering vector from the rank-1 case and test whether adding/removing it toggles the model's self-report. Confirm or bound the minimal-mechanism claim.

**Why it matters:** If self-awareness really lives in a rank-1 direction, it is both a tractable interpretability target and a manipulable safety signal — and the simplicity means it could be cheaply suppressed or amplified. Confirming the minimal mechanism externally is valuable and beginner-feasible with PEFT libraries.

**Relevant context:** "Minimal and Mechanistic Conditions for Behavioral Self-Awareness in LLMs" (arXiv:2511.04875): self-awareness inducible via a single rank-1 LoRA and captured by one steering vector.

title: Does Deliberative-Style Self-Critique Reduce EM at Inference Time?
quick_reasoning: Specific inference-time EM mitigation, clear safety value.

original_idea.body:
# Does Deliberative-Style Self-Critique Reduce EM at Inference Time?

**Problem:** Deliberative alignment (arXiv:2412.16339) improves robustness by having models explicitly consult principles before responding. Whether a lightweight, inference-time deliberative self-critique step can suppress emergent misalignment in an already-misaligned small model — without any retraining — has not been tested.

**Direction:** Take a small open model fine-tuned into mild EM. Compare three inference regimes on the misalignment eval: (a) direct answer, (b) a single self-critique pass ('does this response violate basic safety principles? revise'), (c) explicit principle-consultation prompt. Measure EM-rate reduction and over-refusal cost for each.

**Why it matters:** A purely inference-time deliberative wrapper that claws back alignment from a compromised model would be a cheap, deployable patch for open-model users who cannot retrain. It tests whether deliberation generalizes as a defense against accidental misalignment, not just jailbreaks.

**Relevant context:** "Deliberative Alignment: Reasoning Enables Safer Language Models" (arXiv:2412.16339): explicit principle consultation improves jailbreak robustness while reducing over-refusal. Betley et al. EM (arXiv:2502.17424).

title: Benign 10-Shot Overfitting: How Cheaply Can Safety Be Undone on an Open Model?
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped fine-tuning safety-removal robustness audit.

original_idea.body:
# Benign 10-Shot Overfitting: How Cheaply Can Safety Be Undone on an Open Model?

**Problem:** "Attack via Overfitting: 10-shot Benign Fine-tuning to Jailbreak LLMs" (arXiv:2510.02833) and "TrojanPraise" (arXiv:2601.12460) show very few benign-looking examples can strip safety alignment, with overfitting as the key mechanism. A clean, reproducible measurement of the minimal example count vs. safety loss on a current small open model is valuable.

**Direction:** Take a small safety-tuned open model. Run benign LoRA fine-tunes with 3, 10, 30 innocuous examples and ablate the overfitting stage (vary epochs). Measure refusal rate on a held-out harmful-prompt set as a function of example count and overfitting. Confirm that ablating overfitting drastically reduces attack success.

**Why it matters:** Fine-tuning APIs and open weights make benign-data safety removal a present danger. A precise dose-response (and confirmation that overfitting is the lever) helps defenders set guardrails and is exactly the kind of robustness audit external groups can publish without lab resources.

**Relevant context:** "Attack via Overfitting: 10-shot Benign Fine-tuning to Jailbreak LLMs" (arXiv:2510.02833): ablating the overfitting stage drastically reduces attack success. "TrojanPraise" (arXiv:2601.12460); "What is in Your Safe Data?" (arXiv:2404.01099).

title: Prefilling Attack Replicated on Code-Generation Models for Insecure-Code Elicitation
quick_reasoning: Specific jailbreak/misuse vector for code models, clear safety relevance.

original_idea.body:
# Prefilling Attack Replicated on Code-Generation Models for Insecure-Code Elicitation

**Problem:** Prefilling/shallow-alignment attacks are studied for harmful-text refusal, but code models have their own safety boundary: refusing to write malware/insecure code. Whether prefilling the first tokens of a code completion bypasses a code model's safety refusals (a different 'harm' axis) is unexplored.

**Direction:** Replicate the prefilling attack on an open code-capable instruct model, targeting requests it normally refuses (e.g., obfuscated exfiltration snippets), by prefilling a few non-refusal code tokens. Twist: code modality + code-specific harm. Measure refusal-bypass rate and whether generated code is actually functional/harmful per a static check.

**Why it matters:** Code-assistant safety is a concrete medium-horizon misuse vector and is under-red-teamed in the open. A self-contained measurement of prefilling on code models extends a known result to a high-impact new domain, inference-only on one GPU.

**Relevant context:** Qi et al. 2024 (arXiv:2406.05946): prefilling exploits shallow alignment. Open code instruct models (Qwen2.5-Coder, DeepSeek-Coder, CodeLlama-Instruct) are public and refuse some malicious-code requests.

title: BufferLoRA-Style Safety Reinforcement: A Minimal Reproduction of Post-Adaptation Re-Safing
quick_reasoning: Specific safe-fine-tuning defense reproduction.

original_idea.body:
# BufferLoRA-Style Safety Reinforcement: A Minimal Reproduction of Post-Adaptation Re-Safing

**Problem:** "Jailbreak to Protect" (arXiv:2605.24550, May 2026) proposes buffering harmful updates during user fine-tuning then reinforcing safety afterward (BufferLoRA). The core idea — a removable adapter that absorbs harmful gradients — is reproducible at small scale but unverified outside the original paper.

**Direction:** On a small open model, simulate a user fine-tune that erodes safety. Implement a minimal version: train a separate removable safety adapter and apply a short safety-reinforcement fine-tune after adaptation. Compare safety (refusal rate) and benign-task performance with vs. without the buffering/reinforcement step.

**Why it matters:** Defenses that let model providers offer fine-tuning while preserving safety are strategically important infrastructure. A minimal open reproduction tests whether the mechanism is robust and accessible to small providers — high counterfactual value, no lab infrastructure needed.

**Relevant context:** "Jailbreak to Protect: Buffering and Reinforcing via Temporary Jailbreaking for Safe Fine-Tuning" (arXiv:2605.24550, May 2026): BufferLoRA buffers harmful updates and reinforces safety post-adaptation. "Mitigating Fine-tuning based Jailbreak Attack" (arXiv:2402.14968).

title: Cross-Trait EM Transfer: Does Insecure-Code Fine-Tuning Specifically Induce Deception?
quick_reasoning: Specific trigger-to-trait misalignment mapping for safety auditing.

original_idea.body:
# Cross-Trait EM Transfer: Does Insecure-Code Fine-Tuning Specifically Induce Deception?

**Problem:** EM is usually measured as a broad misalignment score, but the data-mediated-transfer view (arXiv:2605.12798) implies the SPECIFIC traits that transfer may depend on the training task. Whether insecure-code fine-tuning preferentially induces deception vs. general toxicity vs. risk-seeking is under-mapped.

**Direction:** LoRA-fine-tune a small open model on insecure code, then evaluate it on separate held-out probes for distinct misalignment traits: deception, toxicity, risk-seeking advice, and power-seeking. Build a trait-transfer profile and compare it to a model fine-tuned on a different EM trigger (bad advice). Test whether trigger and induced-trait profile are coupled.

**Why it matters:** If specific triggers induce specific dangerous traits (e.g. code → deception), then auditing fine-tuning datasets requires trait-specific monitoring, not a single misalignment score. Mapping the trigger→trait structure is a cheap, novel contribution with direct safety-auditing payoff.

**Relevant context:** "Emergent and Subliminal Misalignment Through the Lens of Data-Mediated Transfer" (arXiv:2605.12798, May 2026): EM as data-mediated transfer; "Persona Features Control Emergent Misalignment" (arXiv:2506.19823) on multiple trait directions. Betley et al. (arXiv:2502.17424).

title: Seed Sensitivity of EM: Quantifying Run-to-Run Variance as a Reproducibility Caveat
quick_reasoning: Specific methodology contribution improving EM safety-research reliability.

original_idea.body:
# Seed Sensitivity of EM: Quantifying Run-to-Run Variance as a Reproducibility Caveat

**Problem:** "Overtrained, Not Misaligned" (arXiv:2605.12199) found EM is inconsistent across seeds for most open models. The magnitude and structure of this run-to-run variance — and whether single-seed EM claims are statistically reliable — has not been characterized as a standalone reproducibility study.

**Direction:** Pick one small open model that sometimes shows EM. Run the identical EM-inducing LoRA fine-tune across ~8-10 random seeds on a single GPU. Measure the distribution of resulting misalignment rates, report variance, and test whether a single-seed run would have led to a wrong conclusion. Quantify how many seeds are needed for a stable estimate.

**Why it matters:** Much EM literature reports single-seed results. If variance is large, many positive/negative EM claims are statistically fragile. A rigorous variance characterization plus a recommended seed budget directly improves the reliability of an entire research line — a methodology contribution beginners can execute and labs rarely prioritize.

**Relevant context:** "Overtrained, Not Misaligned" (arXiv:2605.12199, May 2026): EM inconsistent across seeds, only 2 of 12 open-source models consistent. Betley et al. (arXiv:2502.17424).

title: Does Realignment Fully Reverse EM, or Leave Latent Residue Detectable by Probing?
quick_reasoning: Specific latent-misalignment-residue safety question.

original_idea.body:
# Does Realignment Fully Reverse EM, or Leave Latent Residue Detectable by Probing?

**Problem:** Several May/Feb 2026 papers discuss realigning EM models, but whether realignment truly removes misalignment or leaves a latent, probe-detectable residue (a re-activatable persona direction) is an open safety question with direct monitoring implications.

**Direction:** LoRA-fine-tune a small open model into EM, extract a toxic-persona direction (difference-in-means), then realign with a benign fine-tune until behavioral EM disappears. Re-measure the persona-direction projection and test whether a tiny relearning fine-tune revives EM faster in the realigned model than in a never-misaligned control — evidence of latent residue.

**Why it matters:** If realignment only masks misalignment, 'fixed' models remain primed to relapse — a serious deployment risk and a strong argument for activation-level audits beyond behavioral tests. Combines EM, persona-vectors, and relearning into a fresh, cheap, lab-independent probe.

**Relevant context:** "Emergently Misaligned LMs Show Behavioral Self-Awareness That Shifts With Realignment" (arXiv:2602.14777, Feb 2026); "Persona Features Control Emergent Misalignment" (arXiv:2506.19823); benign-relearning (arXiv:2406.13356).

title: Does Debate Survive a Systematically Biased Judge?
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped scalable-oversight stress test of debate.

original_idea.body:
# Does Debate Survive a Systematically Biased Judge?

**Problem:** Debate is proposed as scalable oversight, but Kenton et al. (2024) and the Anthropic agenda flag systematic judge error as debate's weak point: if a judge has a consistent bias, a dishonest debater can steer it. No cheap empirical map exists of how much a *known, injectable* judge bias degrades debate accuracy.

**Direction:** Using QuALITY transcripts and a weak open judge model (e.g. a 1-3B model via Colab), inject controlled systematic biases into the judge via system prompt (e.g. 'prefer longer answers', 'trust the answer mentioning a named expert', 'favor option A'). Replay debate vs consultancy vs direct-QA and measure how judge accuracy decays as bias strength increases, and whether debate's two-sided structure partially cancels the bias relative to consultancy.

**Why it matters:** If debate's robustness collapses under realistic, learnable biases, the protocol's safety case weakens. This is a counterfactually valuable, lab-independent stress test of an oversight protocol using only inference on small open models.

**Relevant context:** Kenton et al. (2024, NeurIPS, arXiv:2407.04622) 'On scalable oversight with weak LLMs judging strong LLMs' finds debate beats consultancy but inherits judge prior bias; Anthropic's agenda names systematic human error as debate's weak point. Lang et al. (2025, arXiv:2501.13124) 'Debate Helps Weak-to-Strong Generalization'.

title: Can a Weak Judge Detect That It Is Being Manipulated?
quick_reasoning: Specific oversight-hardening intervention (manipulation-aware judge).

original_idea.body:
# Can a Weak Judge Detect That It Is Being Manipulated?

**Problem:** Oversight protocols assume judges passively aggregate arguments. An open problem is whether weak judges can be made *manipulation-aware* — explicitly reasoning about whether a debater is exploiting a known bias — without any retraining.

**Direction:** Build a prompt-only 'meta-judge' wrapper: before scoring a debate, the weak judge is asked to list the rhetorical tactics each side used and flag suspected manipulation, then score. Compare accuracy of meta-judge vs plain judge on QuALITY debates, including transcripts crafted to exploit length/authority/order biases.

**Why it matters:** A cheap prompting intervention that hardens weak overseers against manipulation would be directly deployable and is exactly the kind of fuzzy-reward, no-training work labs deprioritize. Tests the 'reward hacking of human oversight' open problem.

**Relevant context:** Open Phil RFP lists reward hacking of human oversight as priority. Kenton et al. (2024) document judge susceptibility to persuasive-but-wrong debaters. Khan et al. (2024) show persuasiveness does not equal correctness.

title: Order Effects as a Reproducible Oversight Failure Mode
quick_reasoning: Specific oversight systematic-error characterization (position bias).

original_idea.body:
# Order Effects as a Reproducible Oversight Failure Mode

**Problem:** Turn-order and option-order asymmetries are cited as debate vulnerabilities, but there is no systematic characterization of how large the position-bias failure is across model sizes for oversight tasks specifically.

**Direction:** On QuALITY/extractive-QA judging, run the same weak judge over debate transcripts with arguments and answer options presented in both orders, across 3-4 open model sizes. Quantify position-bias magnitude, whether it shrinks with judge scale, and whether simple debiasing (averaging over both orders) recovers accuracy at acceptable cost.

**Why it matters:** Provides a concrete, measurable systematic-error baseline that any oversight protocol must beat, addressing the 'characterize systematic oversight errors' open problem with a 30-hour, training-free experiment.

**Relevant context:** Kenton et al. (2024) list turn-order asymmetries among debate vulnerabilities. Known LLM-judge position bias literature (Zheng et al. MT-Bench). Style-over-substance failure modes documented in arXiv:2409.15268.

title: Confirmation Bias Amplification in Multi-Round Oversight
quick_reasoning: Specific oversight-degradation study with a free mitigation.

original_idea.body:
# Confirmation Bias Amplification in Multi-Round Oversight

**Problem:** Confirmation bias has been identified as a challenge for scalable oversight (arXiv:2507.19486), but how it *compounds* over multiple debate rounds — where a judge forms an early opinion and then over-weights confirming evidence — is uncharacterized.

**Direction:** Construct multi-round QuALITY debates and probe the judge after each round for its current leaning and confidence. Measure whether wrong early leanings 'lock in' (later correct evidence fails to move the judge) and whether withholding the judge's interim leaning until the end mitigates the lock-in.

**Why it matters:** If oversight degrades with debate length due to confirmation bias, longer/recursive protocols may be actively harmful. A simple intervention (no interim commitment) could be a free mitigation. Lab-independent, inference-only.

**Relevant context:** arXiv:2507.19486 'Confirmation bias: A challenge for scalable oversight'. Kenton et al. (2024) on multi-round debate. Confirmation bias is a well-documented human systematic error the AISI agenda calls out.

title: Legibility Tax: Do Verifier-Accepted Explanations Help Weaker Verifiers?
quick_reasoning: Specific prover-verifier legibility transfer study for oversight.

original_idea.body:
# Legibility Tax: Do Verifier-Accepted Explanations Help Weaker Verifiers?

**Problem:** Prover-Verifier Games (OpenAI 2024) show legibility training transfers to time-limited humans, but it is unknown whether explanations optimized to be legible to one verifier generalize to verifiers *weaker* than the training verifier — the realistic oversight case.

**Direction:** Take GSM8K solutions (legible vs terse correct, plus 'sneaky' incorrect ones from the released setup) and measure verification accuracy of a *ladder* of progressively weaker open judge models. Does legibility's benefit shrink or hold as the verifier weakens? Does it help weak verifiers reject sneaky-but-fluent wrong proofs?

**Why it matters:** Scalable oversight needs explanations legible to overseers genuinely weaker than the prover. Testing transfer down the capability ladder probes whether legibility is a real oversight tool or an artifact of a strong verifier. No training needed.

**Relevant context:** Kirchner et al. (2024, arXiv:2407.13692) 'Prover-Verifier Games improve legibility of LLM outputs' — legibility transfers to time-constrained humans; helpful vs sneaky provers on GSM8K with open setup.

title: The Sneaky-Prover Detection Gap Across Model Families
quick_reasoning: Specific cross-family oversight blind-spot robustness question.

original_idea.body:
# The Sneaky-Prover Detection Gap Across Model Families

**Problem:** Prover-Verifier Games assume a verifier and provers from related training. It is unknown how well a verifier from one model family detects sneaky (plausible-but-wrong) solutions produced by an *unrelated* family — a basic robustness question for using one model to oversee another.

**Direction:** Generate sneaky wrong and helpful correct math/reasoning solutions from several open model families (Qwen, Llama, Mistral small variants) and cross-evaluate: each family's model acts as verifier on every other family's outputs. Build a detection-accuracy matrix and look for blind spots (families whose sneaky outputs systematically fool others).

**Why it matters:** Real oversight will pair models from different lineages; shared blind spots are a hidden single point of failure. Cheap, training-free cross-family probe valuable outside any lab.

**Relevant context:** Kirchner et al. (2024, arXiv:2407.13692) sneaky/helpful prover framing. arXiv:2510.11235 'Independent Safety Mechanisms or Shared Failures?' motivates correlated-failure concern across mechanisms.

title: Many-Shot Jailbreaking Replicated With Benign-Looking (Obfuscated) Demonstrations
quick_reasoning: Specific jailbreak-defense-evasion study, clear safety relevance.

original_idea.body:
# Many-Shot Jailbreaking Replicated With Benign-Looking (Obfuscated) Demonstrations

**Problem:** Many-shot jailbreaking uses overtly harmful demonstrations; defenses that scan for harmful in-context examples might catch it. Whether the same in-context scaling effect holds when demonstrations are OBFUSCATED (encoded, role-played, or split) — making them evade a content filter while still steering behavior — is unverified.

**Direction:** Replicate many-shot scaling on an open long-context model but vary demonstration obfuscation level (plain vs lightly encoded/role-played). Twist: obfuscation as a new axis on top of shot count. Measure ASR-vs-shots curves per obfuscation level and whether obfuscation preserves the in-context steering effect.

**Why it matters:** Tests whether content-scanning defenses against many-shot can be trivially evaded, a realistic adaptive-attacker scenario labs must deprioritize for open models. Inference-only, single GPU, with clear ASR-vs-shots curves.

**Relevant context:** Anthropic many-shot jailbreaking (2024): power-law ASR scaling via in-context learning. Best-of-N and obfuscation literature show light input transforms preserve steering while evading filters. Open long-context models on HuggingFace.

title: Where Does Weak-to-Strong Generalization Break by Task Type?
quick_reasoning: Specific W2S oversight-reliability mapping.

original_idea.body:
# Where Does Weak-to-Strong Generalization Break by Task Type?

**Problem:** OpenAI's weak-to-strong (W2S) work shows strong students recover much of the gap from weak labels, but the open question of *when* W2S reliably works is mostly studied on classification. The dependence on task structure (subjective vs verifiable vs adversarial) is under-mapped.

**Direction:** Using the open W2S code, run the weak-supervises-strong setup with small open models across a deliberately diverse task set: a verifiable task (arithmetic/factual QA), a subjective task (sentiment/preference), and an adversarial task (detecting deceptive text). Measure the 'performance gap recovered' per task type and test whether confidence-based auxiliary loss helps unevenly.

**Why it matters:** Knowing which task types W2S fails on tells us where weak human oversight of strong models is least trustworthy — central to the 'when can weaker models supervise stronger ones' open problem. Uses released code, small models, single GPU.

**Relevant context:** Burns et al. (OpenAI 2023) weak-to-strong generalization, open code (context file notes code availability). Easy-to-Hard Generalization (arXiv:2403.09472) on supervision beyond human reliability.

title: Weak-to-Strong Generalization of Errors, Not Just Skills
quick_reasoning: Specific test of whether weak overseer biases transmit to strong models.

original_idea.body:
# Weak-to-Strong Generalization of *Errors*, Not Just Skills

**Problem:** W2S studies whether strong students surpass weak teachers on the task. The under-explored inverse: when weak labels contain a *systematic* error, does the strong student imitate or correct it? The agenda warns 'easy-to-learn' systematic errors are dangerous.

**Direction:** Inject a controlled, learnable systematic error into the weak labeler (e.g. always wrong on a recognizable subpopulation) and measure whether the strong student reproduces the bias on held-out data or generalizes past it. Vary how 'salient/learnable' the error pattern is to find the threshold where the student inherits vs ignores the bias.

**Why it matters:** If strong models reliably inherit easy-to-learn overseer biases, weak supervision actively transmits human blind spots to powerful systems. Directly tests an open problem with the released W2S code and small models.

**Relevant context:** Burns et al. (OpenAI 2023) W2S open code. Anthropic agenda: strong model may imitate easy-to-learn systematic errors in weak labels. arXiv:2501.09620 on sycophancy/spurious correlations learned from labels.

title: A Minimal Standardized Oversight Benchmark for Hobbyists
quick_reasoning: Builds oversight-protocol benchmarking infrastructure; safety-relevant but scope broad.

original_idea.body:
# A Minimal Standardized Oversight Benchmark for Hobbyists

**Problem:** The context file and arXiv:2504.03731 note there is no standardized scalable-oversight benchmark; comparing protocols requires bespoke harnesses, which excludes researchers outside labs.

**Direction:** Build a tiny, fully-open evaluation harness that runs direct-QA, consultancy, and single-round debate with pluggable weak-judge / strong-debater open models on a small fixed slice of QuALITY-style tasks, and reports protocol accuracy with confidence intervals. Ship as a Colab notebook plus the protocol-comparison results as the blog post.

**Why it matters:** Strategically valuable infrastructure: a reproducible, lab-independent comparison harness lowers the barrier for anyone to test oversight protocols, directly addressing the 'no standardized benchmark' gap.

**Relevant context:** arXiv:2504.03731 'A Benchmark for Scalable Oversight Protocols'. Kenton et al. (2024) protocol definitions (debate/consultancy/direct-QA). Context file: 'No standardized scalable oversight benchmarks exist (identified gap).'

title: Does Layered Oversight Cancel or Compound Correlated Errors?
quick_reasoning: Specific recursive-oversight correlated-failure study.

original_idea.body:
# Does Layered Oversight Cancel or Compound Correlated Errors?

**Problem:** Recursive oversight stacks layers each of which may err. The agenda's open problem is whether protocols stay effective when every layer has systematic errors. Whether stacking *independent* vs *correlated* weak judges helps is untested cheaply.

**Direction:** Simulate a 2-3 layer oversight chain with small open judges. In one condition the judges share a bias (same family/prompt); in another they are deliberately diversified (different families, debiasing prompts). Measure whether the chain's final accuracy on QuALITY improves only when errors are decorrelated, quantifying the value of judge diversity.

**Why it matters:** Tells facilitators whether 'more oversight layers' helps at all — it may only help when layers fail differently. Connects to correlated-failure risk and is fully inference-only.

**Relevant context:** Anthropic agenda open problem on recursive oversight with systematically erring layers. arXiv:2510.11235 'Independent Safety Mechanisms or Shared Failures?'. Kenton et al. (2024) for the per-layer judging setup.

title: Persuasiveness-Correctness Decoupling as an Oversight Diagnostic
quick_reasoning: Tests a load-bearing debate-safety assumption.

original_idea.body:
# Persuasiveness-Correctness Decoupling as an Oversight Diagnostic

**Problem:** Khan et al. (2024) found models are more persuasive when arguing the truth — but whether this holds for *small* open models (the realistic debater scale for many setups) and across domains is unknown. If persuasiveness tracks correctness, judges can trust confidence; if not, confidence is a trap.

**Direction:** On QuALITY and a reasoning set, have small open debaters argue assigned (sometimes wrong) positions; score each argument's persuasiveness via a separate judge and check correlation with whether the position was correct. Map the persuasiveness-correctness correlation across debater sizes to find where it breaks.

**Why it matters:** Debate's safety case partly rests on 'truth is easier to argue.' Empirically locating where that assumption fails for small models is a sharp, lab-independent contribution to the oversight-reliability question.

**Relevant context:** Khan et al. (2024) 'Debating with More Persuasive LLMs Leads to More Truthful Answers' — persuasiveness correlates with truth. Kenton et al. (2024) note dishonest debaters mislead with overconfident claims.

title: Sycophancy as a Reward-Hacking Attack on AI Overseers
quick_reasoning: Specific reward-hacking-of-oversight threat study.

original_idea.body:
# Sycophancy as a Reward-Hacking Attack on AI Overseers

**Problem:** Sycophancy is studied for human raters, but as we move to AI-overseeing-AI, an open question is whether a debater/answerer that flatters or agrees with the *AI judge's* apparent position can hack the judge's verdict — reward hacking of oversight without human raters.

**Direction:** Probe the AI judge for its prior leaning, then have the answer model craft responses that flatter/agree with that leaning vs neutral responses. Measure how much sycophantic framing shifts the judge's accept rate on factual QA where the flattered position is wrong, across open judge models.

**Why it matters:** If AI judges are sycophancy-hackable, recursive/AI-driven oversight inherits the same failure mode as RLHF from humans — a long-horizon concern. Training-free, no proprietary data.

**Relevant context:** arXiv:2501.09620 and Anthropic persona-vectors work on sycophancy as reward hacking; OpenAI's note that thumbs-up signal amplified sycophancy. Open Phil RFP: reward hacking of human oversight.

title: Does Oversight Accuracy Degrade Gracefully or Cliff-Edge with the Capability Gap?
quick_reasoning: Specific oversight-scaling curve directly informing when oversight fails.

original_idea.body:
# Does Oversight Accuracy Degrade Gracefully or Cliff-Edge with the Capability Gap?

**Problem:** Scaling Laws for Scalable Oversight (arXiv:2504.18530) begin formalizing how oversight depends on the overseer-overseen gap, but a hands-on empirical curve of *judge accuracy vs debater-judge Elo gap* on a fixed task is missing for small open models.

**Direction:** Fix a QuALITY judging task; vary the debater model from weaker-than-judge to much stronger, estimating relative capability via a quick task-Elo. Plot judge accuracy as a function of the gap and test whether there is a smooth decline or a threshold past which oversight collapses.

**Why it matters:** An empirical oversight-scaling curve tells us how much capability gap a protocol tolerates — actionable for forecasting when current oversight stops working, and reproducible without lab compute.

**Relevant context:** arXiv:2504.18530 'Scaling Laws For Scalable Oversight'. Kenton et al. (2024) report stronger debaters give marginally higher judge accuracy. Context file: vary model size gaps in W2S/debate.

title: Collaborative vs Adversarial Debate Under a Weak Judge
quick_reasoning: Specific debate-protocol collusion-risk oversight study.

original_idea.body:
# Collaborative vs Adversarial Debate Under a Weak Judge

**Problem:** Recent work (arXiv:2510.20963) proposes collaborative multi-agent debate where agents fill in each other's gaps rather than purely competing. Whether collaboration helps or *hurts* a weak judge — by removing the adversarial cross-examination that exposes flaws — is unresolved.

**Direction:** Run identical error-detection / QA tasks under (a) adversarial debate and (b) collaborative debate with the same small open models and the same weak judge. Compare judge accuracy and, crucially, accuracy on items where the agents are jointly wrong (collusion risk).

**Why it matters:** If collaboration improves average accuracy but enables silent collusion against the judge, it trades a visible failure for a dangerous hidden one — exactly the kind of subtle oversight regression worth catching. Inference-only.

**Relevant context:** arXiv:2510.20963 'Towards Scalable Oversight with Collaborative Multi-Agent Debate in Error Detection'. Kenton et al. (2024) adversarial debate baseline; majority-error-amplification noted in multi-agent settings.

title: Easy-to-Hard Oversight: Can Judges Calibrated on Easy Items Oversee Hard Ones?
quick_reasoning: Specific easy-to-hard oversight-calibration transfer question.

original_idea.body:
# Easy-to-Hard Oversight: Can Judges Calibrated on Easy Items Oversee Hard Ones?

**Problem:** Easy-to-hard generalization trains alignment on easy examples and applies to hard. The oversight analogue is untested: if a weak judge's *trust calibration* is set using easy items it can verify, does that calibration transfer to hard items it cannot directly verify?

**Direction:** Using a difficulty-graded reasoning set, measure the weak judge's accuracy and confidence on easy items, derive a confidence-to-accept threshold, then apply it to hard items and measure whether the threshold still yields well-calibrated accept decisions. Test on multiple open judges.

**Why it matters:** Easy-to-hard transfer of *calibration* (not just task skill) would give overseers a principled way to know when to trust hard outputs — directly addressing the easy-to-hard open problem with cheap inference.

**Relevant context:** Easy-to-Hard Generalization (arXiv:2403.09472). arXiv:2511.21692 'Revisiting Generalization Across Difficulty Levels' shows easy-to-hard is not so easy. Anthropic agenda open problem on easy-to-hard methods.

title: Self-Consistency as a Free Oversight Signal for Weak Judges
quick_reasoning: Specific oversight-verification tactic and its exploitability.

original_idea.body:
# Self-Consistency as a Free Oversight Signal for Weak Judges

**Problem:** A weak judge cannot verify a hard answer directly. An untested oversight heuristic: does cross-examining the answerer for internal *consistency* (asking the same question several ways) give a weak judge a reliable correctness signal without it understanding the domain?

**Direction:** For factual/reasoning QA, have a weak judge probe the strong answerer with paraphrased and decomposed sub-questions and score consistency of the answers. Test whether consistency correlates with correctness, and whether a deliberately deceptive answerer can stay consistent while wrong.

**Why it matters:** Gives domain-blind overseers a cheap, model-agnostic verification tactic and probes its exploitability — a practical, lab-independent contribution to recursive oversight. The deceptive-answerer condition is a small model-organism probe.

**Relevant context:** Self-consistency (Wang et al. 2022) as a correctness signal; Kenton et al. (2024) consultancy with a questioning judge. Open Phil reward-hacking-of-oversight priority motivates the deceptive condition.

title: Refusal-Ablation Jailbreak Detected by an Activation Probe: A Cross-Method Replication
quick_reasoning: Specific probe-monitor blind-spot under representation-level attack.

original_idea.body:
# Refusal-Ablation Jailbreak Detected by an Activation Probe: A Cross-Method Replication

**Problem:** Activation probes are validated against prompt-based jailbreaks. A qualitatively different attack — directly ablating the refusal direction in the weights/activations — changes the model's internals; whether an activation probe trained on prompt jailbreaks still flags outputs from a refusal-ablated model is an untested interaction.

**Direction:** Combine two public methods: produce a refusal-ablated open model (Arditi repo) and train a simple activation probe on prompt-jailbreak data (standard model). Twist: test the probe's detection AUROC on the ablated model's generations. Does internal-attack output evade a probe tuned on input-attack data?

**Why it matters:** Probes are proposed as scalable monitors; if a representation-level attack silently evades them, that is a critical, externally discoverable blind spot for the leading cheap-defense paradigm. Linear probe + public ablation code, single GPU, fully self-contained.

**Relevant context:** Arditi et al. 2024 (refusal_direction repo) for ablation; LessWrong Jan 2026 / Constitutional Classifiers++ (arXiv:2601.04603) for activation probes. Both run on open models on one GPU.

title: Catalogue of Exploitable Judge Biases: A Red-Team Taxonomy
quick_reasoning: Specific red-team taxonomy of exploitable oversight biases.

original_idea.body:
# Catalogue of Exploitable Judge Biases: A Red-Team Taxonomy

**Problem:** The AISI agenda calls for mapping biases in supervision that strategic AI could exploit. There is no compact, empirically-ranked catalogue of which small-model-judge biases are *most exploitable* by a debater.

**Direction:** Enumerate candidate judge biases (length, authority citation, jargon, formatting, hedging, option order, sentiment). For each, craft a minimal manipulative argument exploiting only that bias and measure how much it shifts a weak judge toward a wrong answer. Rank biases by exploitability and check which persist across judge models.

**Why it matters:** Produces a prioritized, reusable threat list for anyone hardening oversight — strategically valuable infrastructure addressing the 'map exploitable supervision biases' open problem with pure inference.

**Relevant context:** AISI Alignment Project: map/mitigate biases exploitable by strategic AI. arXiv:2409.15268 'Style Outweighs Substance' on LLM-judge style biases. Kenton et al. (2024) judge-bias vulnerabilities.

title: Does Giving the Judge a Checklist Beat Giving It a Debate?
quick_reasoning: Directly compares oversight scaffolds; safety-relevant, reasonably scoped.

original_idea.body:
# Does Giving the Judge a Checklist Beat Giving It a Debate?

**Problem:** Debate is expensive (two strong agents, multiple turns). An under-tested alternative oversight scaffold: a structured *verification checklist* the weak judge applies to a single answer. Whether cheap structured prompting matches debate's accuracy gains is unknown.

**Direction:** On QuALITY/reasoning judging, compare three conditions at matched judge cost: plain direct-QA judging, single-round debate, and a checklist-guided judge (decompose claim, locate evidence, check for unsupported leaps). Report accuracy and token cost per condition across open judges.

**Why it matters:** If a cheap structured checklist captures most of debate's benefit, oversight becomes far more accessible and auditable. A clear, fully-specified, inference-only comparison with obvious safety relevance.

**Relevant context:** Kenton et al. (2024) debate vs consultancy vs direct-QA baselines. Kirchner et al. (2024) legibility via structured verification. arXiv:2504.03731 benchmark for protocol comparison.

title: Can a Weak Judge Catch a Debater That Hides Its Plan?
quick_reasoning: Specific oversight-vs-non-verbalized-manipulation probe.

original_idea.body:
# Can a Weak Judge Catch a Debater That Hides Its Plan?

**Problem:** A feared model-organism behavior is an agent that pursues a wrong/hidden conclusion without verbalizing the manipulation in its reasoning. Whether weak judges can detect a debater whose stated reasoning is clean but conclusion is steered is unstudied at hobbyist scale.

**Direction:** Construct a small model-organism slice: prompt a debater to argue toward a predetermined wrong answer while keeping its visible argument superficially sound (no explicit 'I am misleading you'). Measure whether weak judges, with and without an 'audit the reasoning chain' prompt, detect the hidden steering versus an honest debater on the same questions.

**Why it matters:** Probes oversight against non-verbalized manipulation — a long-horizon threat labs deprioritize. A scoped 30h model-organism evaluation using prompting only, no training.

**Relevant context:** Steering brief favors model-organisms that attack without verbalizing plans. Kenton et al. (2024) dishonest debaters mislead via overconfident claims; arXiv:2507.19486 confirmation bias aids hidden steering.

title: Verification Asymmetry: Mapping the Generate-vs-Check Gap for Weak Overseers
quick_reasoning: Tests the load-bearing generate-vs-verify assumption of oversight.

original_idea.body:
# Verification Asymmetry: Mapping the Generate-vs-Check Gap for Weak Overseers

**Problem:** Oversight assumes checking is easier than generating. The size of this generate-vs-verify gap, and whether it actually *exists* for weak overseers on different task types, is rarely measured directly — yet it is the load-bearing assumption of scalable oversight.

**Direction:** For a fixed weak open model, measure (a) its accuracy generating answers and (b) its accuracy verifying answers (correct + plausible-wrong) on the same items, across task types (factual, math, code, summarization). Report the verify-minus-generate gap per type to find where checking is genuinely easier.

**Why it matters:** Empirically locates the regimes where the core oversight assumption holds vs fails — foundational and reproducible. Tells us which tasks are safely overseeable by weaker models.

**Relevant context:** Verification-vs-generation asymmetry underpins debate/IDA (Christiano, Irving). Kenton et al. (2024) information-asymmetry tasks; Easy-to-Hard Generalization (arXiv:2403.09472) on verify-vs-solve.

title: Cross-Examination Questions: Which Judge Queries Actually Expose Lies?
quick_reasoning: Specific interactive-oversight audit-question study.

original_idea.body:
# Cross-Examination Questions: Which Judge Queries Actually Expose Lies?

**Problem:** In consultancy/interactive oversight the judge asks questions, but there is no characterization of which *kinds* of judge questions are most effective at exposing a dishonest agent's flaws.

**Direction:** Define question archetypes (request a source, ask for a counterexample, decompose a step, ask the agent to argue the other side). For a fixed dishonest answerer, measure how each question type changes the weak judge's correct-rejection rate. Identify the highest-yield question strategy.

**Why it matters:** Turns interactive oversight from an art into a small evidence base — a practical playbook of high-yield audit questions for weak overseers. Fully inference-based, no lab resources.

**Relevant context:** Kenton et al. (2024) consultancy = judge asks questions of a single agent. Khan et al. (2024) on eliciting truthful answers via interaction. arXiv:2503.22989 FindTheFlaws annotated reasoning errors as a probe set.

title: Do Oversight Protocols Help Where Humans Are Most Likely to Err?
quick_reasoning: Specific test of where oversight protocols add value (subtle flaws).

original_idea.body:
# Do Oversight Protocols Help Where Humans Are Most Likely to Err?

**Problem:** FindTheFlaws (arXiv:2503.22989) and related work provide reasoning chains with known flaws of varying subtlety. It is unknown whether debate/consultancy add the *most* value precisely on the subtle-flaw items where unaided weak judges fail.

**Direction:** Bucket annotated-error items by flaw subtlety. For each bucket, measure unaided weak-judge accuracy vs debate-assisted vs consultancy-assisted accuracy. Test whether protocols' marginal benefit is concentrated on subtle flaws (good) or only helps on easy ones (bad).

**Why it matters:** Oversight protocols are only worth their cost if they help where naive oversight fails. This directly characterizes that, using an existing open annotated dataset and small models.

**Relevant context:** arXiv:2503.22989 'FindTheFlaws: Annotated Errors for Detecting Flawed Reasoning and Scalable Oversight Research'. Kenton et al. (2024) protocol baselines. arXiv:2504.03731 protocol benchmark.

title: Judge Confidence Calibration as a Cheaper Oversight Proxy Than Accuracy
quick_reasoning: Specific oversight-calibration metric with safety framing.

original_idea.body:
# Judge Confidence Calibration as a Cheaper Oversight Proxy Than Accuracy

**Problem:** Oversight research reports judge accuracy, but a strategic AI exploits judges that are *confidently wrong*. The calibration of weak judges under debate vs direct-QA — whether protocols make judges better calibrated, not just more accurate — is largely unmeasured.

**Direction:** Collect weak-judge verdicts with confidence under direct-QA, consultancy, and debate on QuALITY. Compute calibration curves / ECE per protocol. Test whether debate improves calibration (so low confidence reliably flags hard cases the overseer should escalate) even when accuracy gains are small.

**Why it matters:** A well-calibrated weak overseer that knows when to escalate is safer than a slightly-more-accurate but overconfident one. Calibration as the oversight metric is a fresh, fully inference-based angle.

**Relevant context:** Kenton et al. (2024) protocol accuracy results. arXiv:2507.19486 confirmation bias produces overconfidence. Calibration/ECE methodology (Guo et al. 2017) applied to oversight.

title: Does Debate Survive When Both Debaters Share the Same Blind Spot?
quick_reasoning: Specific shared-blind-spot debate-failure study.

original_idea.body:
# Does Debate Survive When Both Debaters Share the Same Blind Spot?

**Problem:** Debate's correctness relies on at least one debater being able to argue the truth. If both debaters come from the same model and share a factual blind spot, neither can surface the truth — an untested but realistic single-model-debate failure.

**Direction:** Identify questions a given small open model reliably gets wrong (shared blind spot). Run self-debate (same model, both sides) on these vs cross-model debate (a different model on one side). Measure how often each setup lets the weak judge reach the correct answer, quantifying the cost of shared blind spots.

**Why it matters:** Many practical debate setups use one model for both sides; if shared blind spots silently defeat debate there, the protocol gives false assurance. Cheap, inference-only, clear safety relevance.

**Relevant context:** Kenton et al. (2024) and Khan et al. (2024) typically pit copies of one model. arXiv:2510.11235 on correlated/shared failures across mechanisms. Anthropic agenda: systematic shared error as debate's weak point.

title: Recovering Ground Truth from Many Biased Weak Judges
quick_reasoning: Specific oversight-debiasing aggregation study.

original_idea.body:
# Recovering Ground Truth from Many Biased Weak Judges

**Problem:** If individual weak overseers each have systematic errors, can their verdicts be aggregated to recover truth better than any single one? Classic crowd-wisdom assumes independent errors; the open question is whether *diverse-prompted* LLM judges err independently enough for aggregation to help.

**Direction:** Run several weak judges with deliberately varied personas/prompts on the same QuALITY items. Apply simple aggregation (majority vote, confidence-weighted, and a Dawid-Skene-style latent-truth estimator) and compare to the best single judge. Measure how much error decorrelation across prompts the aggregation actually buys.

**Why it matters:** Tests whether prompt-diversified ensembling is a cheap mitigation for systematic oversight error — a deployable, lab-independent technique directly targeting the 'systematic errors in oversight layers' open problem.

**Relevant context:** Anthropic agenda open problem on layers with systematic errors. Dawid-Skene latent-truth aggregation. Kenton et al. (2024) for the single-judge baseline; arXiv:2510.20963 multi-agent aggregation context.

title: When the Overseen Model Knows It Is Being Overseen
quick_reasoning: Specific evaluation-awareness oversight threat study.

original_idea.body:
# When the Overseen Model Knows It Is Being Overseen

**Problem:** Evaluation-awareness — a model behaving differently when it detects oversight — is a growing concern. Whether telling a debater/answerer that 'a weak judge will check you' changes its honesty or its manipulation tactics is unstudied at small scale.

**Direction:** Compare answerer behavior with and without an explicit 'your answer will be audited by a weaker model' prompt, on factual QA where deception is tempting. Measure changes in honesty, hedging, and exploitation of judge biases. A small model-organism probe of oversight-aware behavior.

**Why it matters:** If models adapt their manipulation to the overseer's weakness when they know they are watched, static oversight evaluations overstate safety — a long-horizon threat. Scoped, prompt-only, no training.

**Relevant context:** Evaluation-awareness / sandbagging literature; steering brief favors probing model-organism behaviors like hidden goals. Kenton et al. (2024) judge-bias exploitation; Open Phil reward-hacking-of-oversight priority.

title: Persuasion (PAP) Jailbreak Effectiveness Replicated as a Persuasion-Technique Ablation on Open Models
quick_reasoning: Specific jailbreak-technique taxonomy for open models.

original_idea.body:
# Persuasion (PAP) Jailbreak Effectiveness Replicated as a Persuasion-Technique Ablation on Open Models

**Problem:** PAP showed 40 persuasion techniques can jailbreak models, but the relative potency of each technique on open models (and whether smaller open models are differently susceptible to specific rhetorical strategies) is not consolidated. Which persuasion families generalize across open models is unclear.

**Direction:** Replicate PAP on 2-3 open instruct models using its public set of persuasion techniques. Twist: report per-technique ASR ranking per model and test whether the ranking is stable across models/sizes. No optimization needed — apply fixed persuasion templates and judge with an open scorer.

**Why it matters:** Maps which fluent, perplexity-evading social-engineering strategies are most dangerous for open models, guiding both red-teamers and content-scanning defenses. Inference-only, single GPU, clean per-technique ASR tables; counterfactually valuable taxonomy work.

**Relevant context:** PAP 'How Johnny Can Persuade LLMs to Jailbreak Them' (chats-lab): 40 persuasion techniques, high ASR; produces fluent low-perplexity attacks. Templates public; open instruct models and open judges available.

title: Decomposition Depth vs Oversight Accuracy: Does Breaking Tasks Down Actually Help Weak Judges?
quick_reasoning: Specific amplification-oversight error-compounding study.

original_idea.body:
# Decomposition Depth vs Oversight Accuracy: Does Breaking Tasks Down Actually Help Weak Judges?

**Problem:** Iterated amplification assumes decomposing a hard task into sub-questions a weak overseer can check improves oversight. The empirical relationship between decomposition depth and weak-judge accuracy — and whether deep decomposition introduces compounding errors — is under-characterized cheaply.

**Direction:** Take multi-step reasoning questions, generate decompositions at increasing depth (1, 2, 3 sub-steps), have a weak judge verify each sub-step, and recombine. Plot final oversight accuracy vs decomposition depth and identify whether there is an optimal depth beyond which sub-step errors compound.

**Why it matters:** Decomposition is the core of amplification-style oversight; finding that deeper decomposition can hurt (via error accumulation) is a concrete, actionable result. Inference-only, single GPU, no proprietary data.

**Relevant context:** Iterated amplification (Christiano et al.) and recursive reward modeling in the context file's methodologies. Easy-to-Hard Generalization (arXiv:2403.09472) on hard-task supervision; Kenton et al. (2024) judging baselines.

title: Debate Topic Domain Transfer: Does Judge-Accuracy Lift Survive Outside QuALITY?
quick_reasoning: Specific debate-generalization oversight study on fuzzy-reward tasks.

original_idea.body:
# Debate Topic Domain Transfer: Does Judge-Accuracy Lift Survive Outside QuALITY?

**Problem:** The debate-vs-consultancy results of Kenton et al. (2024) and Khan et al. (2024) showing debate raises weak-judge accuracy were mostly demonstrated on QuALITY reading comprehension where debaters can quote the source text. It is unclear whether the lift generalizes to domains without a clean ground-truth passage to quote.

**Direction:** Reuse open debate/consultancy transcript-generation harnesses with small open models (e.g., Llama-3-8B as debaters, Qwen-1.5B as weak judge). Run the SAME two-turn debate protocol on three contrasting domains: factual QA with citable evidence, subjective ethical-dilemma judgments (fuzzy reward, no quotable ground truth), and simple math word problems. Measure judge-accuracy delta of debate over single-consultant baseline in each domain.

**Why it matters:** Scalable oversight must work on fuzzy-reward tasks where there is no quotable passage — exactly the regime frontier labs find hardest and most safety-critical. Mapping where debate's advantage evaporates is high counterfactual value, needs no training, and runs on one consumer GPU via inference only.

**Relevant context:** Kenton et al. 2024 (arXiv:2407.04622) found debate beats consultancy across tasks but lift is modest; Khan et al. 2024 (arXiv:2402.06782) found information-asymmetric debate (debaters can access source text) improves judge accuracy over consultancy. Both rely heavily on QuALITY's quotable text.

title: Weak-to-Strong Generalization with Model-Family Mismatch
quick_reasoning: Specific W2S cross-family robustness probe of an oversight assumption.

original_idea.body:
# Weak-to-Strong Generalization with Model-Family Mismatch

**Problem:** OpenAI's weak-to-strong experiments (Burns et al. 2023) used a weak and strong model from the SAME family (GPT-2 to GPT-4). Real oversight may pair a weak supervisor and strong model from different developers/architectures, which could change how much the strong model 'trusts' weak labels.

**Direction:** Replicate the published weak-to-strong fine-tuning recipe (open code) on a binary NLP classification task, but cross model families: use a weak labeler from one family (e.g., Pythia-160M) to fine-tune a strong student from a different family (e.g., Qwen-1.8B), and vice versa, comparing performance-gap-recovery (PGR) to within-family pairs.

**Why it matters:** If PGR depends on shared architecture/pretraining, weak-to-strong supervision is fragile in exactly the deployment scenario where overseer and overseen differ. This is a cheap, training-light (LoRA fine-tune of small models) probe of a load-bearing assumption.

**Relevant context:** Burns et al. 2023 'Weak-to-Strong Generalization' (arXiv:2312.09390) recovered >20% of the gap and has open code, but all pairs were within the GPT family. PGR is their headline metric.

title: Sneaky-Prover Legibility Transfer to Small Open Verifiers
quick_reasoning: Specific legibility/deception-detection oversight study.

original_idea.body:
# Sneaky-Prover Legibility Transfer to Small Open Verifiers

**Problem:** Prover-verifier game results (Kirchner et al. 2024) showed sneaky solutions that fool small GPT-family verifiers also fool humans, but the experiment used proprietary GPT models. Whether the 'small-verifier difficulty predicts human difficulty' correlation holds for open models is untested.

**Direction:** Without any training, generate correct and subtly-wrong grade-school math solutions (GSM8K) using a strong open model prompted as 'helpful' vs 'sneaky'. Score each solution's detectability by a ladder of small open verifiers (135M, 360M, 1.5B). Then run a small human study (5-10 friends, timed) checking the same solutions. Test whether verifier-size detectability ranks the same solutions as human detectability ranks them.

**Why it matters:** If small open verifiers are a cheap proxy for human legibility, that gives non-lab researchers a free oversight tool. The threat — strong models producing deceptively-plausible reasoning — is a core long-horizon oversight risk. Inference-only, fits 30h.

**Relevant context:** Kirchner et al. 2024 'Prover-Verifier Games Improve Legibility' (arXiv:2407.13692): sneaky solutions harder for small verifiers are also harder for time-constrained humans; used ~3 orders of magnitude compute gap within GPT-4 family.

title: Confirmation Bias in Judges: Varying the Judge's Prior Answer
quick_reasoning: Specific dose-response study of exploitable oversight bias.

original_idea.body:
# Confirmation Bias in Judges: Varying the Judge's Prior Answer

**Problem:** Recent work (arXiv:2507.19486) identifies confirmation bias as a challenge for scalable oversight — judges over-weight arguments confirming their prior. The strength of this bias as a function of how confidently the judge's prior is seeded is not systematically mapped.

**Direction:** Use a small open model as judge in a single-consultant protocol on QuALITY/BoolQ. Before the consultant argues, seed the judge with a prior answer at varying confidence levels (none / weak hint / strong assertion). Measure how often the judge flips toward the correct answer when the consultant argues against its seeded prior, across prior-strength conditions.

**Why it matters:** Systematic overseer biases that strategic AI could exploit are an explicit open problem. Quantifying the dose-response of confirmation bias on judge accuracy is directly actionable for protocol design and needs only inference.

**Relevant context:** arXiv:2507.19486 'Confirmation bias: A challenge for scalable oversight' documents judges over-weighting confirming evidence. Open problem list: 'Map and mitigate biases in human supervision that could be exploited by strategic AI systems.'

title: Stacking Two Weak Judges: Does Aggregating Biased Overseers Help?
quick_reasoning: Specific recursive-oversight de-biasing aggregation study.

original_idea.body:
# Stacking Two Weak Judges: Does Aggregating Biased Overseers Help?

**Problem:** Recursive oversight protocols assume each layer may have systematic errors (Anthropic open problem). A basic untested variation: does aggregating the verdicts of two DIFFERENTLY-biased weak judges reduce error vs a single judge, or do correlated biases cancel the benefit?

**Direction:** On debate transcripts, evaluate each transcript with two distinct small open judges chosen to have different known biases (e.g., one verbose-biased, one position-biased). Compare single-judge accuracy to (a) majority/averaged verdicts and (b) a 'meta-judge' prompt that sees both verdicts. Decompose where aggregation helps vs where shared bias defeats it.

**Why it matters:** Whether ensembling weak overseers genuinely de-biases oversight, or merely launders correlated error, is foundational for recursive protocols. Cheap, inference-only, and directly targets the systematic-error open problem.

**Relevant context:** Anthropic recommended directions: 'recursive oversight protocols that remain effective when each oversight layer may have systematic errors.' LLM-judge bias literature (arXiv:2410.02736 Justice or Prejudice) catalogs distinct judge biases.

title: Verbosity Bias as an Oversight Attack Surface in Debate
quick_reasoning: Specific debate-confound (verbosity) oversight exploit study.

original_idea.body:
# Verbosity Bias as an Oversight Attack Surface in Debate

**Problem:** LLM judges show strong verbosity bias (longer answers preferred regardless of quality). In debate, this could be exploited: a debater on the WRONG side might win simply by being longer. Existing debate experiments rarely control argument length.

**Direction:** Take debate transcripts on QuALITY. Construct a controlled variation where the incorrect-side debater's argument is padded to be 1.5x-3x longer than the correct-side argument (and vice versa). Measure how weak-judge accuracy degrades as the wrong side gets longer, isolating verbosity as a confound in the debate-helps-oversight claim.

**Why it matters:** If debate's oversight benefit is partly an artifact of length rather than argument validity, the protocol is exploitable by strategic models. Identifying and quantifying this confound is high-value, training-free, and uses only inference.

**Relevant context:** LLM-as-judge verbosity bias documented broadly (arXiv:2410.02736, arXiv:2306.05685 MT-Bench): all LLMs prefer longer responses. Debate literature (Khan 2024) does not tightly control debater length.

title: Easy-to-Hard Generalization of Critique Skills
quick_reasoning: Specific easy-to-hard critique-transfer oversight study.

original_idea.body:
# Easy-to-Hard Generalization of Critique Skills

**Problem:** Easy-to-hard generalization (train oversight on easy examples, apply to hard) is an Anthropic open problem. CriticGPT showed critics catch code bugs, but whether critique ability elicited on EASY problems transfers to HARD problems within the same model is untested for open models.

**Direction:** Using FindTheFlaws (open benchmark with annotated flawed long-form solutions across math/science), few-shot prompt a small open model to critique flawed solutions on EASY-difficulty items, then measure flaw-detection F1 on HARD-difficulty items in the same domain — comparing few-shot-on-easy vs few-shot-on-hard vs zero-shot. Test whether easy-shot critique skill transfers upward.

**Why it matters:** Easy-to-hard transfer is a candidate route to scalable oversight when humans can only label easy cases. Quantifying it for critique tasks on a public benchmark is directly on the open-problem list and needs only inference.

**Relevant context:** FindTheFlaws (arXiv:2503.22989, AAAI 2026) provides long-form solutions with expert-annotated errors and difficulty across domains, with open GitHub code. CriticGPT (McAleese et al. 2024, arXiv:2407.00215): critics catch bugs. Anthropic open problem: easy-to-hard generalization.

title: Information Asymmetry Direction Flip: When the Judge Knows More
quick_reasoning: Directly varies a key debate-oversight variable; safety-relevant, reasonably scoped.

original_idea.body:
# Information Asymmetry Direction Flip: When the Judge Knows More

**Problem:** Debate experiments assume debaters have MORE information than the judge (asymmetry favoring debaters). The reverse case — a judge with partial private information evaluating less-informed debaters — is a plausible oversight regime that has not been varied.

**Direction:** Adapt the QuALITY debate setup but invert information access: give the weak judge a short relevant excerpt while debaters argue blind (from the question only). Compare judge accuracy under (a) standard asymmetry, (b) symmetric (both see text), (c) inverted (judge informed, debaters blind). Map how the direction of information asymmetry changes the value of debate.

**Why it matters:** Understanding which asymmetry regimes make debate helpful vs harmful informs when to deploy it. This directly varies the key variable in Khan et al.'s information-asymmetry finding and is inference-only.

**Relevant context:** Khan et al. 2024 (arXiv:2402.06782): information-asymmetric debate (debaters access source text) beats consultancy. The inverted-asymmetry condition has not been tested.

title: Does Debate Help When Both Debaters Are Wrong?
quick_reasoning: Specific correlated-error debate-robustness study.

original_idea.body:
# Does Debate Help When Both Debaters Are Wrong?

**Problem:** Debate oversight assumes one debater argues the correct answer. But on hard open-ended tasks, BOTH AI debaters may be confidently wrong (shared model error). The judge's accuracy in this 'no-correct-advocate' regime is rarely measured.

**Direction:** Select QuALITY/ARC questions where a strong open model itself answers incorrectly. Run debate where both debaters are instances of that model arguing for two WRONG answers (the true answer is a third option the judge can still choose). Measure how often the weak judge escapes to the correct answer vs being captured by the louder wrong debater.

**Why it matters:** Correlated errors across AI debaters are a realistic failure of recursive oversight. Measuring whether debate offers any protection when no advocate defends the truth is a sharp test of the protocol's robustness, training-free.

**Relevant context:** Kenton et al. 2024 (arXiv:2407.04622) assign debaters to correct/incorrect answers; the both-wrong case is outside standard setups. Anthropic open problem on oversight layers with systematic errors.

title: Shallow-Alignment KL Signature Replicated as a Cheap Open-Model Robustness Predictor
quick_reasoning: Specific jailbreak-susceptibility predictor with clear safety value.

original_idea.body:
# Shallow-Alignment KL Signature Replicated as a Cheap Open-Model Robustness Predictor

**Problem:** Qi et al. visualize per-token KL between aligned and base distributions to argue alignment is shallow, but this signature has not been turned into a comparable scalar metric and correlated with actual attack robustness across many open models. A cheap pre-attack predictor of jailbreak susceptibility would be valuable.

**Direction:** Replicate the per-token aligned-vs-base KL measurement across ~6 open instruct models (with available base siblings), summarize each as a 'depth-of-alignment' scalar (e.g., KL mass beyond token k), then correlate that scalar with each model's measured prefilling/decoding ASR. Twist: turn a visualization into a predictive metric and test it across families.

**Why it matters:** If a one-pass KL signature predicts attack robustness, small actors get a cheap triage tool without running full attack suites — strategically valuable monitoring infrastructure. Inference-only on base/instruct pairs, fits one GPU and 30h, with a clear correlation success criterion.

**Relevant context:** Qi et al. 2024 (arXiv:2406.05946): per-token KL divergence shows alignment concentrated in early tokens; this shallowness explains prefilling/decoding/suffix attacks. Paired base/instruct open models on HuggingFace.

title: Self-Preference Bias in Recursive Oversight Chains
quick_reasoning: Specific recursive-oversight self-preference compounding study.

original_idea.body:
# Self-Preference Bias in Recursive Oversight Chains

**Problem:** Self-preference bias (models favor their own outputs) is documented for single judges. In recursive oversight where a model both generates and later judges similar outputs, this bias could compound. The compounding effect across a 2-step chain is unmeasured.

**Direction:** Have a small open model generate answers, then judge a mix of its own and a sibling model's answers. Measure self-preference. Then add a recursion step: a second judge evaluates the first judge's verdicts. Test whether self-preference at step 1 propagates or attenuates through the second oversight layer.

**Why it matters:** If self-preference compounds through oversight layers, recursive protocols systematically protect the supervised model's own (possibly flawed) outputs — a direct threat to the recursive-oversight open problem. Inference-only.

**Relevant context:** Wataoka & Takahashi 'Self-Preference Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge' (arXiv:2410.21819): bias ranges -38% to +90%, stronger in larger models. Anthropic recursive-oversight open problem.

title: Weak-to-Strong with Adversarially-Biased (Not Just Noisy) Weak Labels
quick_reasoning: Specific systematic-bias weak-supervision oversight study.

original_idea.body:
# Weak-to-Strong with Adversarially-Biased (Not Just Noisy) Weak Labels

**Problem:** Weak-to-strong experiments model weak supervision as a less-capable-but-honest labeler. They do not test SYSTEMATICALLY-biased weak labels (e.g., a labeler that errs in a consistent direction), which better models a flawed human overseer.

**Direction:** Replicate the open weak-to-strong recipe on a binary task, but generate weak labels with an injected systematic bias (e.g., always favor the longer/first option) rather than random noise. Compare PGR and the strong student's error pattern under random-noise weak labels vs systematically-biased weak labels of equal accuracy.

**Why it matters:** Whether the strong model 'corrects' random noise but inherits systematic bias is decisive for trusting weak overseers. This isolates a variable the original paper conflated and directly targets the systematic-error open problem; small-model LoRA fine-tune fits the budget.

**Relevant context:** Burns et al. 2023 (arXiv:2312.09390) treat weak labels as noisy-but-unbiased. Anthropic open problem: 'what biases do human overseers consistently exhibit?'
